passages.happening:
“I have made a covenant with my eyes. How then could I gaze with desire at a virgin?” (verse 1). Does God not see his ways and count his every step?

“If I have walked in falsehood or my foot has rushed to deceit, let God weigh me with honest scales, that He may know my integrity” (verses 5-6). If his heart has followed his eyes or his hands are stained, then may another eat what he has sown.

‘If my heart has been enticed by my neighbor’s wife, or I have lurked at his door’ (verse 9), then let his own wife become another man's servant and be taken by other men. ‘For that would be a heinous crime, an iniquity to be judged’ (verse 11), a fire that burns down to destruction.
passages.hearers:
This is the climax of Job's final speech and of all his speeches. Since chapter 9 he has longed for a hearing before God. In chapter 13 he prepared his case, and in chapter 23 he wished he knew where to find God. Here he finally submits it.

The chapter takes the form of an oath of clearance. When a person was accused and no evidence could settle the case, he could swear before God, often with a curse on himself: if he had done this, let such a thing happen to him. Israel's law used oaths in this way. By swearing, the accused put the case in God's hands.

The list begins with the heart. A covenant, berit, is the word used for God's covenants with Noah, Abraham and Israel. Job applies it to the discipline of his own eyes.

The curse of verse 10 is hard to read. It falls on Job's wife, who would have done nothing wrong, picturing her reduced to the work of a slave grinding grain, and worse. It shows how a man's household was bound up with his own name in that world. It is not a picture to approve.
passages.asks: Job's list of sins began with what his eyes looked at. Ask what covenant you would need to make with your own eyes. And ask whether your faithfulness reaches as deep as your heart, or only as far as what others can see.

passages.t: The same One formed master and servant
passages.happening:
“If I have rejected the cause of my manservant or maidservant when they made a complaint against me, what will I do when God rises to judge?” (verses 13-14). “Did not He who made me in the womb also make them? Did not the same One form us in the womb?” (verse 15).

If he has refused the poor what they needed, or let the widow's eyes grow dim with waiting, or eaten his bread alone without sharing it with the orphan, if he has seen anyone die for lack of clothing, or raised his hand against the fatherless because he had friends at the gate, ‘then may my arm fall from my shoulder and be torn from its socket’ (verse 22). ‘For calamity from God terrifies me, and His splendor I cannot overpower’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Household slaves in the ancient world had few rights. Job says he heard their complaints, because he would have to answer to God, and because the same God made master and servant alike in the womb. It is one of the most remarkable verses in the Old Testament on the dignity of every person.

Then come the widow, the orphan and the poor, those with no one to speak for them. Support in the gate means influence among the elders who decided cases. Job swears that he never used his standing to crush someone without it.

This passage answers Eliphaz's charges in chapter 22 one by one.
passages.later: Isaiah names the same deeds as the fast God chooses: ‘to share your bread with the hungry, to bring the poor and homeless into your home, to clothe the naked when you see him’ (Isaiah 58:7).
passages.asks: Job believed that the same God had made him and his servants. Ask whose complaints you are tempted to brush aside because they are below you. And ask whom you eat your bread without.

passages.t: Gold, the sun and moon, and a hidden sin
passages.happening:
“If I have put my trust in gold or called pure gold my security, if I have rejoiced in my great wealth because my hand had gained so much” (verses 24-25), or if he has looked at the sun or the moon in splendor and secretly blown them a kiss in worship, ‘this would also be an iniquity to be judged, for I would have denied God on high’ (verse 28).

He has not rejoiced at his enemy's ruin, or asked for his life with a curse. No stranger had to sleep in the street; ‘my door has been open to the traveler’ (verse 32). And he has not covered his wrongs, as people do, hiding his guilt in his heart for fear of the crowd.
passages.hearers:
The list turns from how Job treated people to how he treated God. Trusting in gold and worshiping the sun and moon are set side by side. Job counts trust in wealth as a form of idolatry, a denial of God.

The worship of the sun and moon was widespread in the ancient world. Throwing a kiss with the hand was a gesture of reverence toward a god. Job says even that secret gesture would have been a denial of God on high.

Hospitality was a solemn duty: householders took in travelers so that no one spent the night in the open street.

In verse 33 Job says he has not hidden his sins like Adam. The word adam is also the ordinary Hebrew word for a human being, so it may mean as people do. Both readings are possible.
passages.later: Elijah was told of the faithful who refused that gesture of worship: ‘all whose knees have not bowed to Baal and whose mouths have not kissed him’ (1 Kings 19:18).
passages.asks: Job named trust in money as a kind of idolatry. Ask what you rely on to feel secure. And ask whether there is anything you are hiding in your heart for fear of what others would think.

passages.happening:
“Oh, that I had one to hear me! Here is my signature. Let the Almighty answer me; let my accuser compose an indictment” (verse 35). He would carry the charge on his shoulder and wear it like a crown. He would give account of every step and come before God like a prince.

And one last oath: if his land cries out against him, if he has eaten its harvest without paying or crushed its tenants, ‘then let briers grow instead of wheat and stinkweed instead of barley’ (verse 40).

‘Thus conclude the words of Job’ (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
Signature translates the Hebrew letter tav, the last letter of the alphabet, written in the older script as a cross mark. Job puts his mark on his defense, like a signature on a legal document, and dares God to write the charge against him.

Many scholars think verses 38 to 40 once stood earlier and have been moved. Others see them as a deliberate last touch that brings the whole oath back to the land and to God's creation.

The narrator's note closes Job's speeches. Everyone now waits for God. Instead, a young man named Elihu steps forward.
passages.later: The same mark is put on the faithful in Ezekiel's vision: “put a mark on the foreheads of the men sighing and groaning over all the abominations committed there” (Ezekiel 9:4).
passages.hard:
Is Job claiming to be sinless?

The oath covers an astonishing range of possible wrongs, and it can sound like a claim to moral perfection. But Job has said elsewhere that no one is pure before God (9:2; 14:4), and he speaks of the sins of his youth (13:26). His oath is not a claim to be without sin. It denies the particular kinds of wrongdoing that could explain his disaster, the guilt the friends insist he must have. In verse 33 he even implies that he has sins, since his point is that he has not hidden them.

Many interpreters also note that Job's standard is very high, reaching to his eyes and his heart. At the same time, the book will show that his confidence in his own goodness led him to speak as though God owed him an explanation, and God will challenge that (40:8). Job is innocent of the charges, as God himself says, but innocence does not give him the right to judge God.
passages.asks: Job signed his case and waited for God to answer. Ask whether you are waiting for an answer from God about something. And ask how you would hold that wait if, like Job, you got an answer different from the one you asked for.
